claims.text: The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy develops larger and more heterogeneous local lattice distortions during deformation than its equiatomic quaternary and ternary FCC subsets.
Greater chemical complexity promotes the formation or evolution of nanoscale short-range chemical order during deformation.
Local lattice distortions encourage the formation and evolution of transient nanoscale ordered clusters.
Transient ordered clusters preferentially form at dislocation intersections or grain boundaries.
Nanoscale chemical ordering modifies dislocation mobility.
Ordered nanoscale features impede dislocation glide.
Atomic-scale chemical heterogeneity can generate variations in generalized stacking-fault energy that coordinate deformation twinning and dislocation slip.
The quinary alloy activates nonconventional slip or twinning more effectively than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The ordering- and distortion-mediated changes in dislocation behavior increase strain hardening and alter plasticity.
Relative to the quinary baseline, equiatomic quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower strain-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary baseline, equiatomic quaternary and ternary alloys will show weaker signals of stress-induced nanoscale ordering.
Evolution of local chemical order in the quinary alloy will correlate with increased dislocation interactions and higher work-hardening capacity.
All compared alloys will begin as homogeneous, single-phase FCC materials with comparable grain sizes and defect densities after identical thermomechanical processing.
High-resolution TEM and APT can assess nanoscale short-range chemical order in these alloys.
Diffuse synchrotron X-ray scattering during deformation can quantify the proposed local lattice distortions.
Using identical processing, room-temperature testing, constant strain rate, and comparable initial microstructures isolates compositional complexity as the primary source of property differences.
